Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission has filed a criminal complaint against Bitkub Online and two former directors, alleging that the crypto exchange submitted daily net-capital reports, known as Form DA 1, that failed to show the effect of a 2021 theft involving about 1.7 billion baht (roughly $53 million) in customer assets.

The July 23, 2026, complaint to Thailand's Economic Crime Suppression Division names Sakolkorn Sakavee and Thaweesap Rawan, who the SEC said were responsible for the reports when they were Bitkub directors. The regulator alleges that Bitkub gave false statements and that the two former directors made false entries in company documents.

Related Reading Dutch crypto exchange collapses exposing customer balances' true value amid multi-million-euro hole The court found an undisclosed deficit and said Knaken cannot repay customers in full, leaving recovery to an independent trustee. Jul 17, 2026·Liam 'Akiba' Wright

According to the SEC, a May 2021 cyberattack caused customer assets across 16 cryptocurrencies to be withdrawn from the exchange. Bitkub's Form DA 1 reports from May 10 through Oct. 30, 2021, showed no material change in its asset balance from the theft, conduct the regulator said amounted to false reporting.

The SEC said subsequent information indicated that Bitkub began procuring replacement digital assets on Oct. 31, 2021. The regulator did not say when that replacement process was completed.

In its response to the complaint, Bitkub acknowledged that personnel responsible for company disclosures chose not to reveal that assets from one company wallet had been stolen. The company said the decision was intended to prevent a bank run while Bitkub was trying to replace the assets. It disputed that the accused individuals had acted fraudulently.

In a separate September 2025 update, the SEC said customer digital assets held by Bitkub were safe and complete as of Sept. 8, 2025. That finding covered a later point in time and did not settle the regulator's allegation about what Bitkub reported in 2021.

Asset replacement and regulatory reporting remain separate questions in the complaint. Bitkub says the nondisclosure was intended to avert a bank run; the SEC alleges that the daily reports failed to show a material change in the exchange's assets before replacement began.

An inquiry official will now investigate and decide whether to recommend prosecution, according to the SEC's criminal-action process. A public prosecutor would then consider the file, and a court would adjudicate the allegations only if the case is brought. The allegations remain unadjudicated.

Thai SEC says Bitkub concealed a 2021 theft for nearly six months, while the exchange says the decision was intended to prevent a bank run.

Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission has filed a criminal complaint against Bitkub, the country’s largest crypto exchange, and two former directors over reports submitted after a previously undisclosed 2021 hack.

The regulator said hackers stole crypto worth about 1.7 billion baht (or approximately $51 million) from Bitkub in May 2021. Still, daily filings submitted between May 10 and October 30 showed no material change in the company’s assets, according to the SEC. The regulator said:

“The SEC further found that Bitkub did not report to the SEC in its daily net capital report (Form DA 1) in a manner consistent with the theft incident.”

Form DA 1 reports are used by the regulator to track an exchange’s financial position. The SEC alleged that Bitkub’s reports therefore contained false information and gave the impression that customer assets were being held normally and that the company had suffered no damage.

Sakolkorn Sakavee and Thaweesap Rawan, Bitkub’s directors at the time, were responsible for submitting the reports and were named alongside the company in the complaint.

Bitkub acknowledged in a statement that people responsible for its disclosures had “decided not to disclose” that one of the company’s wallets had been stolen. It said the decision was intended “to prevent a bank run.” The exchange added:

“Had a bank run occurred, customers could have suffered widespread losses, and Thailand’s digital-asset industry could also have been harmed.”

Bitkub also said the incident “did not result from fraudulent conduct” by those named in the complaint. The crypto exchange added that its co-founders later absorbed the loss by buying the same cryptocurrencies in the same amounts, although the stolen assets were never recovered.
